Diversify

/dih-VUR-suh-fye/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Diversify means to make something varied; to add variety or different kinds of elements to it.

Her financial adviser urged her to diversify, spreading her savings across stocks, bonds, and real estate instead of betting everything on a single company.

Worked Example

After months of selling nothing but grilled cheese, Marcus decided to diversify his food truck's menu, adding tomato soup, three kinds of salads, and a rotating dessert special. Regulars who had grown bored began returning and bringing friends.

Marcus takes a menu that was all one thing and adds several different kinds of items to it, and that act of adding variety is exactly what it means to diversify.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

vary: To vary something is to introduce changes so it is not always the same, and the changes can stay within one kind: varying the route, the pace, the seasoning. To diversify is stronger — it adds genuinely different kinds of elements, changing what the thing is made of.

broaden: To broaden something is to widen its range or reach while it stays the same kind of thing, the way a course can cover more topics. To diversify is to change the makeup itself, bringing in new and genuinely different kinds of elements.

expand: To expand something is to make it larger — more size, more volume, more amount. Something can expand while staying entirely one kind of thing, which is why expanding is not the same as diversifying, which means adding genuinely different kinds of elements to the mix.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

standardize: to make everything conform to one model

narrow: to reduce something to a smaller range

Where it sits · how deeply the makeup is changed — supplement → diversify → overhaul

supplement vs. diversify: To supplement something is to add a little more of what it already has, while to diversify it is to add genuinely different kinds of elements.

overhaul vs. diversify: To diversify something is to widen its variety, but to overhaul it is to tear the whole thing down and rebuild it from the ground up.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — di-

Prefix — di-: apart, in different directions (from Latin dis-)

Root — vers

Root — vers: from Latin vertere, to turn

Suffix — -ify

Suffix — -ify: to make, to cause to become

Put it together

Put it together: Diversify combines di-, a form of Latin dis- meaning 'apart' or 'in different directions,' with the root vers, from vertere, 'to turn,' plus -ify, 'to make.' To diversify something is literally 'to make it turn in different directions,' pushing one uniform thing out toward many different kinds.

Use the root in a new word: versatile

Use the root in a new word: versatile: The versatile actor could turn from comedy to tragedy in a single evening, showing the same Latin 'turning' root, vertere, that lives inside diversify.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, common in business and finance

Diversify often appears in economic contexts, as in 'diversify a portfolio' or 'diversify the local economy,' but it works anywhere variety is being added, from menus to music playlists. Remember that it names a process, an action someone takes, so it always describes adding variety to something, not the state of already having it.
